title: TLSRPT (RFC 8460) failure reporting for MTA-STS and DANE
description:
## What

RFC 8460 TLS Reporting. A recipient domain publishes a reporting endpoint; senders send it daily JSON summaries of TLS negotiation and policy-validation failures.

Not in scope for the MTA-STS work and never claimed: it is a separate RFC. Filed because the hooks now exist and because it is the half of MTA-STS deployment that makes `testing` mode useful.

## Why it matters more than it sounds

`mode: testing` exists so a domain can deploy MTA-STS and find out what would have broken BEFORE enforcing. Without a sender population that reports, testing mode tells the domain nothing -- it is just a policy that does not apply. §5: "Sending MTAs that also implement the TLSRPT specification send a report indicating policy application failures (as long as TLSRPT is also implemented by the recipient domain); in any case, messages may be delivered as though there were no MTA-STS validation failure."

So a sender that implements MTA-STS without TLSRPT is a free rider on the domains that do: it gets the protection and contributes nothing to anyone else's rollout.

## The hooks already exist

PolicyOutcome::is_validation_failure is true for BOTH FailedEnforce and FailedTesting, which is exactly the reportable set -- the distinction testing mode exists to create. There is a test asserting the two predicates disagree precisely on testing, so that surface is already pinned.

SmtpTransportSecurity::Forbidden carries SmtpTransportDenial, which says whether DANE or MTA-STS refused. RFC 8460 reports on both mechanisms, so that distinction is already the right shape.

## Pieces

TXT DISCOVERY. `_smtp._tls.<domain>` TXT, `v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:...` or `rua=https://...`. Same shape as _mta-sts, so pkix-mta-sts-resolver's lookup is the obvious model; whether it belongs in that crate or its own is part of this work.

REPORT AGGREGATION. Per (policy domain, reporting day) counts by failure type. §4.4 defines the result types: starttls-not-supported, certificate-host-mismatch, certificate-expired, certificate-not-trusted, validation-failure, tlsa-invalid, dnssec-invalid, dane-required, sts-policy-fetch-error, sts-policy-invalid, sts-webpki-invalid. Mapping FetchError and SmtpDaneFailure onto those is most of the design.

REPORT SERIALISATION. §4 JSON, gzipped, §5.1 filename convention.

DELIVERY. §3 says SMTP or HTTPS POST. The SMTP path means sending mail from inside a mail library, which is a dependency question worth deciding deliberately.

## The thing to be careful about

A report says which of a domain's MX hosts failed TLS for which sender. That is operational detail about a third party, sent to an address that third party nominated in unsigned DNS. §7 covers it. Worth deciding what is omitted rather than reporting everything available, and worth not treating the rua address as trusted just because it came from the domain it describes.

## Acceptance

[ ] Decide scope: discovery + aggregation + serialisation, with delivery left to the caller, or all four
[ ] `_smtp._tls` TXT discovery with the rua endpoints parsed, and a decision recorded on which crate it lives in
[ ] A mapping from FetchError, SmtpDaneFailure and PolicyOutcome onto §4.4's result types, with the unmapped cases named
[ ] §4 JSON serialisation with a round-trip test against the RFC's own example report
[ ] Document what is deliberately omitted from a report and why (§7)
[ ] A test that a `testing`-mode failure is reported AND delivered, since that pairing is the whole point of the mode
